title: Food Waste: Why It Matters
summary: How much food never gets eaten on its way from farm to table, the water, land, and fuel wasted along with it, and simple ways families and stores can waste less.
poll: Families and stores should work harder to waste less food.

versions.title: Food Waste: Why It Matters
versions.text:
Think about an apple growing on a farm. Not every apple gets eaten. Some fall and stay on the ground. Some go to a store but never get sold. Some sit in a kitchen too long and go bad. All of this food becomes waste.

Food waste happens in many places. It happens on a farm. It happens in a store. It happens in a home, too.

Food waste is a big problem. A farm uses water to grow food. A farm uses land, too. Trucks use fuel to bring food to a store. When food is wasted, we waste water, land, and fuel, too.

Wasted food can cause another problem. It gets thrown in a dump. There, it slowly rots. It can make a bad gas. That gas can trap heat.

You can help at home. Buy only what you need. Store fruit so it stays fresh. Eat your leftover food. Do not throw it out.

Stores can help, too. They can sell fruit that looks odd. They can give extra food to people in need. That way, less food goes to waste.

versions.title: Food Waste: Why It Matters
versions.text:
What happens to food that people never eat? Think about an apple growing on a farm. Not every apple that grows will end up on a plate. Some apples fall from the tree and are left behind after the harvest. Some travel all the way to a store but are never bought. Some sit in a kitchen too long and quietly go bad. All of this uneaten food becomes waste, and food waste is a real problem in almost every country.

Food waste can happen at several different points. It can happen on a farm, in a store, or right in someone's home. Each of these points adds to the overall problem.

Growing food takes many valuable resources. A farm needs water to grow crops, and it needs land to plant them in. Trucks and ships need fuel to carry food from farms to stores. So when food is wasted, every bit of that water, land, and fuel is wasted right along with it.

Wasted food can cause another problem, too. When it is thrown into a dump, it slowly rots there. As it rots, it releases a gas that can trap heat in the air.

Families can take simple steps to cut down on food waste. Buying only the food they truly need, instead of more than they can eat, is a smart first step. Storing fruit and vegetables properly so they stay fresh longer also helps a great deal. Eating leftover food, rather than tossing it out, keeps good food from going to waste.

Stores help too, by selling odd-looking fruit at a lower price and by giving any surplus food to people who need it. In this way, less food across the whole country ends up being wasted.

versions.title: Food Waste: Why It Matters
versions.text:
What happens to food that is grown but never eaten? Around the world, a surprising amount of food never makes it from the farm to a plate. Some crops are left behind after the harvest because they look odd or are slightly damaged, even though they are still safe to eat. Some food spoils on the long trip to a store. Some sits on a shelf past its sell-by date and is eventually discarded. Some is bought by a family but never eaten before it spoils at home. All of this uneaten food is called food waste. Experts think close to a third of all food grown on Earth is wasted somewhere along the way.

Food waste matters because growing food uses a lot of resources. A farm needs water to irrigate its fields, and it needs land to plant its crops. Trucks, ships, and planes burn fuel carrying food over long distances. When food is wasted, those resources are wasted too, since no one gets to eat the food they helped produce.

There is a second cost as well. When wasted food is buried in a landfill, it slowly rots and gives off a gas that traps heat in the air.

Families can waste less food by planning their meals ahead, storing food that spoils quickly the right way, and eating leftovers instead of discarding them. Stores can help by discounting food when its sell-by date is near, and by donating surplus food to people who need it. Small choices like these can add up to real savings of water, land, and energy.

versions.text:
What happens to food that farmers grow but that never reaches a dinner plate? Around the world, a surprisingly large share of food never travels successfully from the farm to the table. This gap between production and consumption is one of agriculture's most persistent problems. Some crops are left behind after the harvest because they look oddly shaped or slightly damaged, even though they remain safe to consume. Some food spoils during the journey from a farm to a store, and some remains on a shelf past its sell-by date and is eventually discarded. Some is purchased by a household but never consumed before it spoils in the kitchen. All of this uneaten food is classified as food waste, and experts estimate that close to one-third of all food produced on Earth is wasted somewhere along this long and complicated journey.

Food waste matters because producing food consumes natural resources. Farmers need water to irrigate their fields and land on which to cultivate their crops. Trucks, ships, and airplanes consume fuel transporting food across long distances. When food is wasted, these resources are squandered too, since nobody benefits from food that required so much effort to produce.

There is a second environmental cost worth considering: wasted food that is buried in a landfill decomposes without oxygen and releases a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere, slowly affecting the whole planet.

Households can mitigate food waste by planning meals in advance, storing perishable items correctly, and consuming leftovers instead of discarding them unnecessarily. Stores contribute to more sustainable consumption by discounting food nearing its sell-by date and donating surplus food to people experiencing hunger. Small choices, repeated by millions of people around the world, accumulate into genuine, measurable savings of water, land, and energy, savings that matter more every single year.

versions.title: Food Waste: Why It Matters
versions.text:
Food waste represents one of the most significant and solvable inefficiencies in global agriculture; a surprisingly substantial proportion of food produced worldwide never actually travels successfully from farm to table, leaving a persistent gap between what is produced and what is ultimately consumed.

This gap opens at multiple points along the journey from farm to plate. Some crops are left behind after the harvest simply because they appear oddly shaped or slightly damaged, even though they remain perfectly safe to consume. Additional food spoils during the lengthy journey from a farm to a distribution center or store, while other food remains on a shelf past its sell-by date and is eventually discarded. Still more food is purchased by a household but never consumed before it spoils in the kitchen. Researchers estimate that close to one-third of all the food produced on Earth is wasted somewhere along this journey, a proportion that surprises many people who assume waste happens mainly in the home.

Food waste matters tremendously because producing food consumes substantial natural resources that are themselves often scarce and unevenly distributed around the world. Farmers require water to irrigate their fields and land on which to cultivate their crops, while trucks, ships, and airplanes consume considerable fuel transporting food across vast distances to reach distant markets. When food is wasted, every one of these resources, the water, the land, and the fuel, is squandered as well, since nobody ultimately benefits from food that required so much effort and energy to produce in the first place.

A second significant environmental cost deserves consideration: wasted food that is buried in a landfill gradually decomposes without oxygen and releases gases that trap heat within the atmosphere, contributing measurably to a warming planet and to broader concerns about overall consumption of the planet's resources.

Fortunately, households and businesses alike can meaningfully mitigate food waste by adopting more sustainable habits. Families can plan meals in advance, store perishable items correctly, and consume leftovers rather than discarding them unnecessarily. Stores contribute to more sustainable consumption patterns by discounting food nearing its sell-by date and donating surplus food to organizations that assist people experiencing hunger. Small individual choices, repeated by millions of people across the globe, accumulate into genuine and measurable savings of water, land, and energy, savings that matter even more in regions where these resources are already severely limited.

Concern about food waste is hardly a modern phenomenon. Long before refrigerators existed, ancient societies relied on drying, salting, and underground storage pits to preserve harvests and prevent them from spoiling before they could be consumed, demonstrating that preventing food waste has mattered to farming communities for thousands of years, across vastly different climates, economies, and cultures.

versions.title: Food Waste: Why It Matters
versions.text:
Food waste constitutes one of the most significant, persistent, and arguably most solvable inefficiencies within global agriculture; a surprisingly substantial proportion of all food produced worldwide never actually travels successfully from farm to table, leaving an enduring and economically costly gap between what is produced and what is ultimately consumed by people.

This troubling gap opens at multiple distinct points along the extended journey from farm to plate. Some crops are deliberately left behind after the harvest simply because they appear oddly shaped or slightly damaged, even though they remain perfectly safe and nutritious to consume. Additional quantities of food spoil during the often lengthy journey from a farm to a distribution center or retail store, while other food remains sitting on a shelf past its printed sell-by date and is eventually discarded without ever being purchased. Still further quantities of food are purchased by an ordinary household but are never actually consumed before spoiling quietly in the kitchen. Researchers estimate that close to one-third of all the food produced on Earth each year is wasted somewhere along this extended journey, a strikingly large proportion that surprises many people who mistakenly assume that most waste happens only in the home.

Food waste matters tremendously because producing food in the first place consumes substantial natural resources that are themselves frequently scarce and unevenly distributed around the globe. Farmers require considerable water to irrigate their fields and valuable land on which to cultivate their crops, while trucks, cargo ships, and airplanes consume enormous quantities of fuel transporting food across vast distances to reach distant and often unfamiliar markets. When food is ultimately wasted, every single one of these resources, the water, the land, and the fuel, is squandered as well, since nobody ever benefits from food that required so much cumulative effort and energy to produce in the first place.

A second, equally significant environmental cost deserves careful consideration: wasted food that is buried deep within a landfill gradually decomposes without access to oxygen and consequently releases methane and other gases that trap considerable heat within Earth's atmosphere, contributing measurably to a warming planet and to broader concerns about sustainable consumption of the planet's limited resources.

Fortunately, households and businesses alike can meaningfully mitigate this widespread problem through more sustainable habits. Families can plan their meals carefully in advance, store perishable items correctly, and consistently consume leftovers rather than needlessly discarding them. Stores, for their part, contribute to considerably more sustainable patterns of consumption by discounting food that is nearing its sell-by date and by donating genuinely surplus food to organizations that assist people experiencing hunger. Small individual choices, faithfully repeated by millions of people across the globe, ultimately accumulate into genuine and measurable savings of water, land, and energy, savings that matter even more urgently in regions where these particular resources are already severely limited.

Concern about food waste is hardly a distinctly modern phenomenon. Long before mechanical refrigerators ever existed, ancient societies across many different continents relied extensively on drying, salting, and underground storage pits to preserve their hard-won harvests and prevent them from spoiling before they could eventually be consumed, clearly demonstrating that preventing food waste has mattered profoundly to farming communities for many thousands of years, across vastly different climates, economies, and cultures.

questions.stem: A family throws away food that spoiled in their kitchen before they could eat it. What is the most likely reason?
options: They grew the food themselves
They bought more food than they could use in time
They donated the food to a store
They stored the food in a landfill
questions.why: The article says food purchased by a household can spoil before it is eaten, often because too much was bought.

wrong.A: Growing food themselves is not mentioned as a cause of spoiling.
wrong.C: Families donate to others, not to stores.
wrong.D: Families store food in kitchens, not landfills.

questions.stem: Why does wasted food in a landfill add gases to the air?
options: Because trucks burn it
Because stores add chemicals to it
Because it rots without air and releases gas
Because sunlight turns it into gas instantly
questions.why: The article says wasted food buried in a landfill decomposes and releases gases that trap heat.

wrong.A: The article does not say trucks burn the food.
wrong.B: The article does not mention stores adding chemicals.
wrong.D: The article does not describe sunlight causing instant change.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the article?
options: By comparing two kinds of farms
By listing countries with the most farms
By telling a story about one apple
By explaining where waste happens, why it matters, and how to reduce it
questions.why: The article moves from where food waste happens, to why it matters, to ways to reduce it.

wrong.A: The article does not compare two kinds of farms.
wrong.B: The article does not list countries by number of farms.
wrong.C: The apple is only a brief example, not the whole structure.

MID.prompt: Explain two ways people can reduce food waste and why each way helps. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained at least two ways to reduce food waste.
I used details from the article to show why each way helps.
I used linking words such as first, next, and because.
MID.modelAnswer: First, families can plan their meals and store perishable food correctly, because this keeps fruit, vegetables, and other food fresh long enough to be eaten instead of thrown away. Next, stores can donate surplus food to people who need it instead of discarding it, because that way food does not go to waste just because its sell-by date is near. These steps matter because they both save the water, land, and fuel that were used to grow and transport the food in the first place.

keyWords.definition: the act of using up food, energy, or other resources
keyWords.example: Turning off lights saves energy and lowers electricity consumption.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without running out or causing serious harm
keyWords.example: Planting a new tree for every one that is cut down is a sustainable practice.

keyWords.definition: to make a problem less serious or severe
keyWords.example: Wearing a helmet can mitigate injuries while cycling.

keyWords.definition: likely to spoil or decay quickly
keyWords.example: Milk and fish are perishable foods that must be kept cold.

keyWords.definition: a large area of land where garbage is buried
keyWords.example: The city built a new landfill outside of town for its trash.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Farms produce too much food and should grow less.
Food waste squanders resources used to produce food and harms the environment.
Only wealthy countries waste food.
Stores should never sell discounted food.
questions.why: The article explains that wasted food squanders water, land, and fuel, and contributes to landfill gases.

wrong.A: The article focuses on reducing waste, not reducing what farms grow.
wrong.C: The article discusses the problem as global, not limited to wealthy countries.
wrong.D: The article says discounting food nearing its sell-by date helps reduce waste.

questions.stem: Roughly what share of food produced on Earth is wasted, according to the article?
options: About one-tenth
About two-thirds
Nearly all of it
About one-third
questions.why: The article states that researchers estimate close to one-third of food produced is wasted.

wrong.A: One-tenth is much lower than the article's estimate.
wrong.B: Two-thirds is higher than the article's estimate.
wrong.C: The article does not claim nearly all food is wasted.

questions.stem: Besides water and land, what other resource does the article say is wasted along with uneaten food?
options: Sand
Glass
Fuel
Paint
questions.why: The article says fuel used to transport food is also wasted when food is wasted.

wrong.A: Sand is not mentioned as a wasted resource.
wrong.B: Glass is not mentioned as a wasted resource.
wrong.D: Paint is not mentioned as a wasted resource.

questions.stem: "Households can mitigate food waste." What does mitigate mean here?
options: Lessen
Increase
Ignore
Celebrate
questions.why: Mitigate means to make something less severe, and the article describes ways to lessen food waste.

wrong.B: Mitigate does not mean to increase a problem.
wrong.C: Mitigate means addressing a problem, not ignoring it.
wrong.D: Mitigate has nothing to do with celebrating.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that resources used to grow food are "unevenly distributed"?
options: To argue that farms should be built only in rich countries
To explain why some farms are bigger than others
To suggest that food never spoils in dry regions
To show that wasting food can hurt regions where resources are already scarce
questions.why: Because some regions already have limited water and land, wasting food there has a bigger impact.

wrong.A: The article does not argue farms should only exist in rich countries.
wrong.C: The article does not claim food never spoils in dry regions.

questions.stem: Why might a landfill produce more heat-trapping gas than a farm field would?
options: Because landfills receive more sunlight than fields
Because buried food decomposes without oxygen there
Because landfills are colder than farm fields
Because landfill food is never organic
questions.why: The article explains that buried food decomposes without oxygen in a landfill, releasing heat-trapping gases.

wrong.A: Sunlight in a landfill is not discussed.
wrong.D: Landfill food, including spoiled produce, is organic.

questions.stem: Why do researchers consider the gap between food production and consumption a serious problem?
options: Because it means farmers grow too little food
Because it causes food prices to drop sharply
Because it means resources used to grow food go to waste
Because it stops trucks from carrying any food
questions.why: When food produced is not eaten, the resources that went into producing it are wasted too.

wrong.A: The gap is about food not being eaten, not about too little being grown.
wrong.D: Trucks still carry food; the gap is about what happens after.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe ancient methods of preserving food, such as drying and salting?
options: To show that preventing food waste is a long-standing human concern
To prove that refrigerators are a modern invention
To argue that old food-storage methods were unsafe
To explain how salt is mined
questions.why: The article uses this history to show that people have long worked to prevent food from spoiling and being wasted.

wrong.B: Refrigerators are mentioned, but not as the article's main point.
wrong.C: The article does not call these methods unsafe.

HIGH.prompt: Should schools and stores be required to donate surplus food instead of discarding it? Take a position and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe schools and stores should be required to donate surplus food instead of discarding it. One piece of evidence is that producing food uses significant resources, such as water, land, and fuel, and throwing away edible food wastes all of those resources for nothing. Another piece of evidence is that food buried in a landfill decomposes without oxygen and releases gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, so donating surplus food instead of discarding it would reduce this environmental cost while also helping people who are experiencing hunger.
